summary: S4 is the Ti-microalloyed, low-density nano-bainitic Al–C steel of the study (C 0.87 wt.%, Al 5.76 wt.%, plus 0.78 wt.% Ni and 0.10 wt.% Ti), austenitized at TA = 1150 °C for 15 min and then austempered at TB = 320 °C for 3500 s to obtain a nano-bainitic microstructure. It is the sample of the investigation designed to trade a slightly lower C–Al level for improved transformation kinetics, ductility and a better strength–ductility balance, and the one in which Ti-microalloying was used to accelerate bainite nucleation and suppress deleterious carbides.
composition: Nominal composition of steel S4 (wt.%): C 0.87, Al 5.76, Mn 0.97, Si 0.30, Mo 0.48, B 0.0026, Ni 0.78, Ti 0.10 (Table 1); Ni and Ti are absent from the sibling steels S1–S3, and Ti is unique to S4. The design intent is a low-density concept in which Al (5.76 wt.%, ~1.3 % density reduction per wt.% Al) stabilises ferrite, suppresses carbide precipitation and refines low-temperature bainitic lamellae; C was deliberately reduced relative to S1–S3 (0.87 vs 0.98–1.10 wt.%) to accelerate the bainitic transformation and mitigate brittleness, with 0.78 wt.% Ni added to prevent polygonal ferrite (αp) formation that the lower C would otherwise promote; Mn (≈1 wt.%) is kept low, Si (0.30 wt.%) remains low because Al also suppresses carbides, Mo (0.48 wt.%) improves hardenability and B (0.0026 wt.%) further raises hardenability without penalising bainite transformation. Ti (0.10 wt.%) microalloying is applied to enhance bainitic transformation and mechanical properties via Ti–Mo–C complex carbides.
processing: Cast steel blocks were produced by vacuum arc furnace casting, then homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to promote uniform composition and microstructure. The homogenized steel was step-by-step hot rolled, reducing thickness to ~11 mm, and slow cooled in the oven. Cylindrical specimens (∅5 × 10 mm³) for heat treatment were cut by water jet (OMAX 2626). The thermal cycle (DIL 805A dilatometer) applied to this sample was: heating at 10 K/s to an austenitizing temperature TA = 1150 °C holding 15 min; cooling at 100 K/s — fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations — down to the austempering temperature TB = 320 °C; isothermal bainitic hold at 320 °C for 3500 s, the near-complete bainitic transformation time (Bt) taken from the onset of the RLC plateau; then final cooling to room temperature. The incubation time was 50–60 s for all S4 parameters. For this alloy 1150 °C was selected because it removes polygonal ferrite down to a trace level (<1.0 %); an additional 1250 °C schedule (15 min) was also tested to dissolve nanoscale MC/TiC precipitates and relieve sheaf impingement. Tensile specimens were heat-treated with the same cycle in the dilatometer.
microstructure: The final microstructure is a markedly fine, dense nano-bainitic sheaf/needle structure of bainitic ferrite (α), with a true lamellar thickness Lt(t) = 36 nm (SD 12 nm), much finer than the 56 nm obtained at TB = 350 °C. Retained austenite (γr, fcc) amounts to 26 % and is mainly film-like at the bainitic lath boundaries; only a trace of polygonal ferrite (αp, bcc, <1.0 %) is present, and AlN appears as minor dark angular particles. XRD Rietveld micro-strains are εγ = 0.58 % and εα = 0.60 %, with no significant difference between the two phases at this condition, i.e. no pronounced heterogeneous dislocation partitioning. The dominant precipitate is needle-shaped, longitudinally aligned TiMoC (Ti–Mo–C complex carbide), confirmed by EDX as Fe-depleted and C/Ti/Mo-enriched, with an absence of micro-defects inside the carbides; (Fe,M)xCy (cementite-like) and MoC are strongly suppressed relative to S1–S3 because of the counter-coarsening effect of TiMoC, and κ-carbide was not detectable microscopically (limited Mn ≈1 wt.%). The fine, dense sheaf/needle structure at 320 °C produces a correspondingly dense interface network (TiMoC/matrix and AlN/matrix boundaries), while the fine prior austenite grain size at 1150 °C is the origin of bainitic sheaf impingement; the increase in phase-boundary density accelerates bainite nucleation but slows the later transformation progression.
properties: Tensile testing on ASTM E8 sub-size round specimens (12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length; Zwick/Roell machine, 250 kN load cell) after dilatometric heat treatment gives, for TA 1150 °C / TB 320 °C, an ultimate tensile strength of 1360 MPa with 10 % total elongation, i.e. a product of strength and elongation (PSE) of 13,600 MPa·% — the highest average total elongation and the best PSE measured in the study. Under the equivalent 1150 °C/350 °C condition S4 reached 1470 MPa with 9.1 % (PSE 13,380 MPa·%), and the 1250 °C/350 °C schedule gave ~1410 MPa with 8.3 % (PSE 11,700 MPa·%). The martensite-start temperature measured by cooling dilatometry at 100 K/s from TA = 1150 °C is Ms = 305 °C (310 °C after austenitizing at 1250 °C), so TB = 320 °C lies just above Ms. Characterization techniques applied to the steel set include light optical microscopy (LOM), SEM, EDX, EBSD, XRD with Rietveld refinement (ASTM E975-13), dilatometry and MatCalc equilibrium/kinetic (TTP) simulations.
mechanisms: Ti microalloying in S4 forms TiMoC complex carbides that act as nucleation sites for bainite sheaves, shortening the incubation time to 50–60 s across all S4 parameters (shorter than the 80–210 s of S1/S2), but the accompanying increase in the number of various phase boundaries causes bainitic sheaf impingement that progressively suppresses bainite progression after incubation, giving Bt = 3500 s at TB 320 °C instead of the much shorter times expected from nucleation alone.

TiMoC forms during the cooling stage after casting and is aligned longitudinally by subsequent hot forming, so secondary precipitation during austempering is negligible (consistent with TTP calculations and the absence of new precipitates within SEM resolution); its self-nucleated complex carbide is more thermodynamically and structurally stable than discrete TiC/MoC and suppresses the formation of (Fe,M)xCy, MoC and probably κ-carbide.

The fine prior austenite grain size produced at 1150 °C promotes impingement, so a higher austenitizing temperature (1250 °C) is used to dissolve nanoscale MC/TiC precipitates and relieve impingement, thereby facilitating relatively faster phase transformation (Bt reduced to 2600 s at 1250 °C/350 °C).

Choosing TB just above Ms (TB 320 °C vs Ms 305 °C) refines the bainitic lamellae (Lt(t) = 36 nm vs 56 nm at 350 °C), which raises strength, while the lower austempering temperature also lowers the retained-austenite fraction (26 % vs 25–29 % range) and thus limits TRIP-assisted strain hardening.

Lowering C to 0.87 wt.% with 0.78 wt.% Ni addition keeps the αp content at a trace level (<1.0 %) without disturbing bainitic transformation kinetics, which is the microstructural basis for S4 raising elongation (10 %) relative to the higher-C, higher-Al S1–S3 and thereby achieving the best strength–ductility balance despite lower UTS.

At TB 320 °C the bainitic ferrite and retained austenite micro-strains are nearly equal (εγ 0.58 % vs εα 0.60 %), indicating no pronounced heterogeneous dislocation distribution between phases; such balanced strain avoids the early strain localisation that, in contrast, in S3 at low TB (εγ 0.54 % vs εα 0.33 %) cuts elongation to 2.4 %.

Because (Fe,M)xCy and MoC are suppressed by TiMoC and the TiMoC particles contain no micro-defects and do not form micro-voids, precipitation does not degrade ductility in S4; the mechanism is one of nucleation-controlled (not spinodal) formation of carbides during prior processing rather than during austempering.
conclusions: Within the tested window Ti-microalloyed S4 is the alloy that offers the best overall strength–ductility balance: at TA 1150 °C / TB 320 °C it reaches UTS 1360 MPa with 10 % elongation and the highest PSE of the steel set (≈13,600 MPa·%), comparable to or better than S1/S2 despite its lower C content. Ti addition coarsens MoC into complex TiMoC carbides formed above the austempering temperature, suppresses more deleterious (Fe,M)xCy/MoC (and probably κ-carbide) and refines the microstructure; S4 nevertheless shows bainitic transformation kinetics similar to S1/S2 (initially fast nucleation, later slowed by sheaf impingement). Overall the study concludes that TB primarily tunes the UTS–elongation trade-off through plate thickness and retained-austenite stability, that the 8.08 wt.% Al design (S3) is detrimental to ductility at low TB, that C variations near 1 wt.% are secondary to Al level, and that the Ti + Ni alloying in S4 compensates the lower C by raising elongation and PSE — supporting the use of such low-density nano-bainitic Al–C steels for high-strength, weight-saving applications.
